title: Functionalization of $g$-wave altermagnets: spin-splitter effect enabled by surfaces
abstract: We investigate surfaces of a $g$-wave altermagnet(AM) and show that they provide a platform for realizing $d$-wave altermagnetism and the associated spin-splitter functionality. Using the Kubo formalism applied to a minimal slab model, we evaluate the spin-splitter effect(SSE) by computing the spin conductivity corresponding to a transverse spin current induced by a longitudinal electric field. We find a finite SSE, absent in the bulk, that emerges from surface-induced $d$-wave altermagnetism. Strikingly, the sign pattern of the $d$-wave altermagnetism on both surfaces of the slab geometry is identical to each other, leading to additive contributions to SSE from the two surfaces, with a spin-splitter angle reaching up to 15 degrees. In addition, this response is intrinsically linked to an accompanying surface-induced weak ferromagnetism, which potentially enables control of altermagnetic domains via an external magnetic field and provides a route to optimize the SSE functionality. These results can be understood in terms of a bulk-boundary correspondence between surface states and bulk altermagnetic order parameters, where the magnetic multipolar character of the latter plays a central role. Our findings strongly suggest thin-film engineering as a viable strategy to functionalize non-$d$-wave AMs.
summary: The authors demonstrate that the surfaces of g-wave altermagnets can be engineered to exhibit d-wave altermagnetism, enabling a measurable spin-splitter effect (SSE) absent in the bulk. Using the Kubo formalism on a minimal slab model, they show this surface enhancement is constructive and linked to induced weak ferromagnetism, suggesting thin-film engineering as a viable route for functionalizing such materials.
main_problem: To realize and study the spin-splitter effect (SSE) in altermagnets (AMs), overcoming the difficulty of finding metallic d-wave AMs at ambient conditions.
main_result: The surfaces of a g-wave altermagnet slab induce d-wave altermagnetism, leading to a finite SSE that is absent in the bulk. This surface response can be engineered via thin-film methods.
method: The Kubo formalism is applied using a minimal single-orbital tight-binding model to compute spin conductivity and characterize the SSE angle.
model_or_system: The study uses a minimal slab model based on a g-wave altermagnet, which incorporates hopping terms ($t_{1,k}, t_{2,k}, t_{3,k}, t_{AM,k}$) and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) terms. The system is analyzed in the context of surface effects.
key_observables: Spin conductivity ($\sigma_{S_z, yz}$), SSE angle ($	heta_{aa}$), weak ferromagnetism ($M_y$), and d-wave spin splitting in the electronic spectrum.
important_parameters: The maximum spin-splitter angle reached was up to 15 degrees. The analysis depends on the magnetic multipolar character of the AM order parameter.
main_assumptions: The SSE is fundamentally linked to the magnetic multipolar character of the AM OP, and the calculations rely on a minimal slab model approximation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the surface d-wave splitting enabling SSE (absent in bulk), plot $\sigma_{S_z, yz}$ vs. chemical potential for varying film thicknesses, and show layer-resolved weak ferromagnetism ($M_y$).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical platform (g-wave AM surfaces) and theoretical framework (Kubo formalism). It then calculates the SSE, demonstrating its surface origin via thickness dependence. Finally, it links this effect to induced weak ferromagnetism, suggesting material engineering strategies.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical mechanism for enhancing magnetic functionalities (SSE) in topological/magnetic materials by exploiting boundary effects, which is highly relevant for designing next-generation spintronic devices.
